questions: How do testimony, incentives, network structure, and opportunities for criticism affect expert agreement?

The role of criticism and independence

evidence.excerpt: Let us now turn to three paradigms in formal social epistemology: the credit economy, network models, and models of epistemic diversity.
Truth seekers might all herd onto the most promising problem in science, while credit seekers will choose less popular topics where they are more likely to be the one generating a finding.

Higginson and Munafo (2016) and Romero (2017) argue that the priority rule strongly disincentivizes scientists from performing replications because credit is so strongly associated with new, positive findings.

Bright (2017a), though, uses a model to point out that credit-seekers who fear retaliation may publish more accurate results than truth-seekers who are convinced of some fact, despite their experimental results to the contrary.
Because famous scientists are more trusted, their discoveries do more good.
On the positive side, besides possible benefits to division of labor, the priority rule incentivizes sharing in science.
If investigators using these poor methods train their students into them, and then place those students disproportionately, they will tend to proliferate.
Another paradigm, widely used by philosophers to explore social aspects of epistemology, are epistemic network models.

For this reason, philosophers of science have tended to use the network epistemology framework introduced by economists Bala and Goyal (1998) to model how more rational individuals learn from neighbors.
As this model progresses these agents gather data, which increases their neighbors’ degrees of belief in turn.
In tightly connected networks, misleading evidence is widely shared, and may cause the community to pre-emptively settle on a poor theory.
This supports central claims from social epistemology espoused by Goldman (1999).

sources.annotation: Surveys credit and network models, including the conditions under which communication promotes or impedes inquiry.

used_for: The role of criticism and independence

evidence.excerpt: Traditional notions of objectivity as faithfulness to facts or freedom of contextual values have also been challenged from a feminist perspective.

Often but not always, feminist epistemologists go beyond pointing out what they regard as androcentric bias and reject the value-free ideal altogether—with an eye on the social and moral responsibility of scientific inquiry.
Longino assigns a crucial function to social systems of criticism in securing the epistemic success of science.

Even the most implausible beliefs might be true, and even if they are false, they might contain a grain of truth which is worth preserving or helps to better articulate true beliefs (Mill 1859 [2003: 72]).
Feminist standpoint theory builds on these ideas but focuses on gender, racial and other social relations.

The perspectival stance can also explain why criteria for objectivity often vary with context: the relative importance of epistemic virtues is a matter of goals and interests—in other words, standpoint.

This idea she refers to as “strong objectivity” replaces the “weak” conception of objectivity in the empiricist tradition: value-freedom, impartiality, rigorous adherence to methods of testing and inference.
To whom does the condition of equally shared intellectual authority apply?

sources.annotation: Distinguishes value-free ideals, inductive risk, social criticism, and the specific protections and limits of randomization.
